title: The Anti-Slide Revolution: Why Sometimes I Swap My Clicker for a Camera
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele makes a research-backed case for embracing the visualiser (document camera) as a primary delivery tool — not a retrograde choice but a strategy that reduces cognitive load and increases responsiveness. He traces a burnout chain that begins with lesson planning and ends with teachers leaving, then argues that pre-prepared slides often violate Cognitive Load Theory's Redundancy Principle and Split-Attention Effect (Sweller) by forcing students to process two language streams at once. Live modelling under a visualiser, he argues, shows novices the struggle and the thinking rather than a magic 'pop-up' answer (Craig Barton), enforces natural pacing that respects the Transient Information Effect, enables genuinely responsive teaching (Adam Boxer), and supports immediate 'Show Call' feedback on real student work (Teach Like a Champion). He advocates a hybrid AI-plus-camera workflow — AI-generated Do Now questions and tailored worksheets, live visualiser modelling for the main lesson — and dismisses the 'eye-contact myth,' noting students never even noticed he had stopped using slides.
points: Pre-prepared slides often violate Cognitive Load Theory's Redundancy Principle and Split-Attention Effect, overloading working memory with two simultaneous language streams.
Live modelling under a visualiser shows novices the struggle and the thinking process, not a 'magic' pop-up answer, and enforces natural pacing aligned with the Transient Information Effect.
The visualiser enables responsive teaching — inventing a fresh example on the spot — and immediate 'Show Call' feedback by placing a student's actual work under the camera.
A hybrid strategy keeps AI for generated Do Now questions and tailored worksheets while reserving the main I Do/We Do teaching for live visualiser modelling.
The 'eye-contact myth' is false: looking down to write means looking at exactly what students see (Shared Attention), and students didn't even notice slides had gone.
quotes: When text appears on a screen while you are speaking, students’ working memory is overloaded trying to process two language streams simultaneously.
On a slide, the answer just “pops up.” It looks like magic. Under a visualiser, students see the physical act of setting out the work.
You cannot write faster than a student can think. When you write live, you naturally slow down to the students’ processing speed.
If a class is confused, a slide deck is a prison. With a visualiser, I can grab a fresh sheet of paper, invent a new example, or draw a diagram from a different angle instantly.
Since making this switch, I noticed something surprising: My students didn’t even notice I stopped using slides.
When I look at the screen, I am looking at exactly what they are looking at.
